los.text: Describe the clinical features of diabetic ketoacidosis and explain how these relate to the underlying pathophysiology and management.
los.html:
• Pathophysiology: absolute insulin deficiency + high counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines, GH):
ProcessConsequenceClinical feature
↑ Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, ↓ glucose uptakeHyperglycaemia → glycosuria → osmotic diuresisPolyuria, thirst, dehydration (often 5–8 L deficit): tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucosa
Unrestrained lipolysis → free fatty acids → hepatic ketogenesis (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate)High anion gap metabolic acidosisKussmaul breathing, "pear drop" (acetone) breath, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, drowsiness → coma
Insulin lack and acidosis shift K⁺ out of cells; losses in urine and vomitTotal body K⁺ depleted even if serum K⁺ is normal or highRisk of hypokalaemia once insulin starts
CatabolismWeight loss
PrecipitantsInfection, missed insulin, new diagnosis, MI, alcohol, pregnancy, SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA).
Diagnosis (JBDS)Ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L (or urine ++), glucose >11 mmol/L or known diabetes, and pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L.
Severe(consider HDU)
  • Ketones >6
  • Bicarbonate <5
  • pH <7.0
  • K⁺ <3.5 on admission
  • GCS <12
  • Sats <92%
  • Systolic BP <90
  • HR >100 or <60
  • Anion gap >16.
ManagementDetail
Fluids
  • 0.9% sodium chloride: 500 mL bolus if systolic <90
  • Otherwise 1 L over 1 h
  • Then 1 L over 2 h
  • 2 h
  • 4 h
  • 4 h
  • 6 h (more cautious in the young, elderly, heart failure)
InsulinFixed-rate IV insulin infusion (soluble insulin) 0.1 units/kg/h; continue the usual long-acting basal insulin
Potassium (per litre of fluid)K⁺ >5.5: none; 3.5–5.5: 40 mmol/L; <3.5: senior review, more potassium
GlucoseAdd 10% glucose at 125 mL/h when glucose <14 mmol/L (keep insulin running to clear ketones)
Targets
  • Ketones fall ≥0.5 mmol/L/h, bicarbonate rise ≥3 mmol/L/h, glucose fall ≥3 mmol/L/h
  • Hourly glucose and ketones, VBG at 1, 2 h then 2-hourly
OtherTreat the precipitant, VTE prophylaxis, catheter if oliguric, NG tube if vomiting and drowsy, fluid balance, specialist diabetes team
ResolutionKetones <0.6 and pH >7.3: switch to SC insulin with a meal, stopping the infusion 30–60 min later
  • Complications: hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema (especially children: headache, confusion, bradycardia), aspiration, VTE, ARDS.

los.text: Describe the key investigations used in the diagnosis and monitoring of type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis.
los.html:
TestDiagnostic threshold
Random glucose with symptoms≥11.1 mmol/L
Fasting glucose≥7.0 mmol/L
2-hour OGTT≥11.1 mmol/L
HbA1c≥48 mmol/mol (not reliable for rapid-onset type 1, children, pregnancy, haemoglobinopathies)
  • Type 1 diagnosis (NICE NG17): clinical: hyperglycaemia with ketosis
    • rapid weight loss
    • young age
    • BMI <25
    • personal or family autoimmunity (don't rule out type 1 because of age or BMI).
    • Same-day specialist referral (children: same day to the paediatric diabetes team).
    • If atypical: autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin) and C-peptide (low; best after 3 years), MODY genetic testing.
MonitoringDetail
HbA1c every 3–6 monthsTarget ≤48 mmol/mol (individualised)
Capillary glucoseTargets: waking 5–7, before meals 4–7, after meals 5–9 mmol/L
Continuous glucose monitoringOffered to all adults and children with type 1 (NICE); time in range (3.9–10 mmol/L) >70%
Blood ketonesDuring illness (sick day rules)
Annual review
  • Weight
  • BP
  • Lipids
  • eGFR and urine ACR
  • Retinal screening
  • Foot check (monofilament, pulses)
  • TFTs (autoimmune)
  • Coeliac screen if symptoms
  • Injection sites (lipohypertrophy)
  • Hypoglycaemia awareness
  • Mood/eating disorders
  • Driving
  • DKA investigations: glucose
    • blood ketones
    • VBG (pH, bicarbonate, K⁺)
    • U&E
    • FBC (WCC often high without infection)
    • CRP
    • cultures
    • urinalysis
    • CXR
    • ECG (K⁺ effects, MI)
    • pregnancy test.

los.text: Explain the pathophysiology of type 1 diabetes and how this relates to its clinical presentation, diagnosis, and long-term management.
los.html:
• Pathophysiology: T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of β-cells in genetically susceptible people (HLA-DR3/DR4), possibly triggered by environmental factors (viruses)
    • autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, insulin, ZnT8) appear years before symptoms.
StageFeatures
1≥2 autoantibodies, normal glucose
2Autoantibodies + dysglycaemia
3Symptomatic diabetes, when ~80–90% of β-cells are lost
Presentation
  • Peak at 10–14 years but any age (LADA in adults)
  • Polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia (bedwetting in children), weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, thrush
  • a quarter or more present in DKA (more in young children).
  • A "honeymoon" period may follow starting insulin (residual β-cell function).
Long-term management follows from absolute insulin deficiency
  • Lifelong insulin (basal–bolus or pump)
  • Carbohydrate counting (DAFNE)
  • CGM and hybrid closed-loop systems
  • Hypoglycaemia management
  • Screening for associated autoimmune disease (thyroid, coeliac, Addison's, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo)
  • and complication prevention: the DCCT trial showed intensive control cuts microvascular complications (with lasting "metabolic memory" and fewer CV events later)
  • at the cost of more hypoglycaemia.
  • Islet or pancreas transplant for severe hypoglycaemia unawareness or with a kidney transplant.

los.text: Link the key functional and morphological features of type I diabetes to its clinical signs and symptoms.
los.html:
Normal isletβ-cells (insulin, ~60–70%), α-cells (glucagon), δ-cells (somatostatin), PP cells.
Morphology in type 1
  • Insulitis (lymphocytic, mainly CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration of islets), then pseudo-atrophic islets with no insulin-containing cells
  • α-cells preserved → unopposed glucagon
  • Smaller pancreas.
Loss of insulin actionSign or symptom
↓ glucose uptake (GLUT4 in muscle and fat), ↑ hepatic glucose outputHyperglycaemia; glucose exceeds the renal threshold (~10 mmol/L) → glycosuria → polyuria, thirst, dehydration
↑ lipolysis and proteolysisWeight loss, muscle wasting, fatigue
↑ ketogenesis (with glucagon)Ketoacidosis: vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, acetone breath
Osmotic changes in the lensBlurred vision
Glucose impairs neutrophils, feeds fungiThrush, skin infections
K⁺ moves out of cellsHigh serum K⁺ despite total body depletion
  • Chronic hyperglycaemia
    • → advanced glycation end-products, polyol (sorbitol) pathway, PKC activation, oxidative stress
    • → microvascular basement membrane thickening: retinopathy (microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, new vessels), nephropathy (hyperfiltration → mesangial expansion, Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules → albuminuria → CKD), neuropathy (glove and stocking, autonomic: gastroparesis, postural hypotension, erectile dysfunction)
    • and accelerated atherosclerosis.

los.text: Describe how the system in Wales works with regards to the assessment of new drugs and the process to decide their availability (or not) for prescribing.
sessions: Resource Allocation in a Pharmacy context
los.html:
Body / processRole in Wales
MHRALicenses medicines for the UK (quality, safety, efficacy)
NICE technology appraisalsApply in Wales as well as England: NHS Wales must make NICE-recommended medicines available (within 2 months of publication)
All Wales Medicines Strategy Group (AWMSG)
  • Appraises new medicines for clinical and cost-effectiveness (using QALYs) when NICE hasn't published guidance
  • Recommendations are mandatory for health boards (also within 2 months)
  • Supported by the All Wales Therapeutics and Toxicology Centre (AWTTC)
One Wales processInterim decisions for medicines (including unlicensed/off-label uses) with no NICE or AWMSG guidance, so access is consistent across Wales
Health board formulariesLocal lists of approved medicines; national prescribing indicators
Individual Patient Funding Requests (IPFR)For a medicine not routinely available: funded if there is evidence of significant clinical benefit and reasonable value for money for that patient
Cost-effectivenessTypically judged against a threshold of about £20,000–30,000 per QALY, with flexibility for end-of-life and rare conditions.
Why it mattersDecisions balance clinical benefit against opportunity cost to the NHS budget, aiming for equitable, consistent access across Wales (avoiding a "postcode lottery").

los.text: Describe the principles of management of type 1 diabetes, including acute and long-term treatment strategies.
los.html:
Acute problemManagement
DKASee LO 1
Hypoglycaemia (<4 mmol/L): autonomic (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) and neuroglycopenic (confusion, drowsiness, seizures)
  • Conscious and can swallow: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g. 150–200 mL fruit juice, 4–5 glucose tablets)
  • Recheck after 10–15 min, repeat up to 3 times, then a starchy snack.
  • Can't swallow/unconscious: IM glucagon 1 mg or IV glucose (e.g. 10% glucose 150–200 mL over 15 min).
  • Don't omit the next insulin
  • Find the cause
Sick day rules
  • Never stop basal insulin
  • Check glucose and ketones every 2–4 h
  • Extra rapid-acting insulin according to ketones
  • Drink fluids
  • Seek help if ketones rising or vomiting (ketones ≥3 → hospital)
Surgery / nil by mouthContinue basal insulin (often reduced), VRIII if missing more than one meal
Long-term strategyDetail
Insulin regimenBasal–bolus: long-acting (detemir, glargine, degludec) + rapid-acting analogue with meals; insulin pump (CSII) or hybrid closed loop
Structured educationDAFNE: carbohydrate counting, insulin dose adjustment
MonitoringCGM, HbA1c ≤48 mmol/mol (individualised), avoid hypoglycaemia (impaired awareness: Gold score)
Cardiovascular riskStatin (e.g. over 40, diabetes >10 years, nephropathy), BP control, ACE inhibitor/ARB if albuminuria, stop smoking
Complication screeningAnnual review (eyes, feet, kidneys)
PsychologicalDiabetes distress, depression, eating disorders (insulin omission)
Life
  • Driving (tell DVLA if on insulin with complications; check glucose before driving, "above 5 to drive")
  • Exercise and alcohol adjustments
  • Pregnancy planning (HbA1c <48, folic acid 5 mg)
  • Transition from paediatric to adult care
  • Adjuncts: metformin may be considered if BMI ≥25 to reduce insulin dose.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of insulin and relevant evidence to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
TypeExamplesOnsetPeakDurationUse
Rapid-acting analogueInsulin aspart (NovoRapid; Fiasp faster), lispro (Humalog), glulisine10–15 min1–2 h3–5 hMealtime bolus, correction doses, pumps
Short-acting (soluble)Actrapid, Humulin S30 min2–4 h6–8 hIV infusions (FRIII/VRIII); 20–30 min before meals
Intermediate (isophane/NPH)Humulin I, Insulatard1–2 h4–8 hUp to ~16–24 hBasal (often twice daily), type 2
Long-acting analogueGlargine (Lantus, Toujeo), detemir (Levemir), degludec (Tresiba, >40 h)1–2 hFlat~24 hBasal once (detemir often twice) daily
Premixed (biphasic)NovoMix 30, Humalog Mix, Humulin M3Twice daily with breakfast and evening meal
Mechanism
  • Insulin binds its tyrosine kinase receptor → IRS → PI3K → GLUT4 translocation (muscle, fat), glycogen and fat synthesis
  • Inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis and ketogenesis
  • Drives K⁺ into cells.
Analogue designAmino acid changes stop hexamers forming (rapid-acting), make insulin precipitate at body pH (glargine), or add a fatty acid that binds albumin (detemir, degludec).
Adverse effects
  • Hypoglycaemia, weight gain, lipohypertrophy (rotate sites; erratic absorption), hypokalaemia (IV), rarely allergy
  • Prescribing errors ("units" in full, correct brand and device, never draw up insulin in an IV syringe, beware concentrated U200/U300/U500).
Evidence and choice
  • DCCT (intensive insulin reduced microvascular complications but tripled severe hypoglycaemia)
  • Long-acting analogues cause less nocturnal hypoglycaemia than NPH
  • Pumps and closed-loop systems improve HbA1c and time in range.
  • Choose by lifestyle, hypoglycaemia risk, ability and preference.
Doses
  • Total daily dose roughly 0.5–1 unit/kg, ~half basal and half bolus
  • Mealtime doses from an insulin:carbohydrate ratio (e.g. 1 unit per 10 g) plus a correction factor.

los.text: Interpret clinical data sets (e.g. blood results, ECGs, imaging, observations) within a gamified, interactive format, applying clinical reasoning to select appropriate responses
los.html:
• Gamified data interpretation: practise a systematic approach for each data type:
DataSystem
ABGpH → PaCO₂ → HCO₃⁻ → primary disorder → compensation → anion gap → PaO₂ against FiO₂
ECGRate, rhythm, axis, P waves, PR, QRS, ST segments, T waves, QT
CXRPatient details, projection, adequacy; airway, breathing (lungs, pleura), cardiac, diaphragm, everything else (bones, lines)
BloodsFBC (MCV pattern), U&E (AKI, Na⁺/K⁺), LFT (pattern), TFT, glucose/ketones; compare with baseline
ObservationsNEWS2 score and trend, escalation
  • Reasoning: link the data to the clinical story, state the most likely diagnosis, and choose the next step (as in the quiz).

los.text: Demonstrate structured wrist and hand examination, hip examination, knee examination and foot and ankle examinations.
los.html:
• General structure: introduce, consent, expose, position
    • look → feel → move → special tests → function → neurovascular
    • examine the joint above and below
    • compare sides.
  • GALS screen (gait, arms, legs, spine) for a quick overview.
JointKey steps
Wrist and hand (ICM Year 1 › Musculoskeletal › LOs 2 and 9)Look (deformity, wasting, nodules, nails), feel (MCP squeeze, snuffbox), move (fist, wrist flexion/extension), function (grip, pinch, button), median/ulnar/radial tests, Phalen's, Tinel's, Finkelstein's
Hip (ICM Year 1 › Musculoskeletal › LOs 10 and 14)Gait (antalgic, Trendelenburg), Trendelenburg test, leg lengths (true/apparent), internal rotation at 90° flexion, Thomas's test
Knee (ICM Year 1 › Musculoskeletal › LO 7)Alignment (varus/valgus), quadriceps wasting, effusion tests (patellar tap, sweep), joint line tenderness, range, Lachman's, drawer tests, collateral stress, McMurray's
Foot and ankle (ICM Year 2 › Musculoskeletal › LO 11)Standing alignment, tiptoe, gait; malleoli, base of 5th MT, Achilles; dorsiflexion/plantarflexion, subtalar, 1st MTP; Simmonds' test; monofilament, pulses

los.text: Analyse clinical findings in the context of anatomical knowledge to identify potential underlying pathologies affecting the wrist and hand, hip, knee or foot and ankle.
los.html:
JointFindingAnatomy → pathology
HipGroin pain, reduced internal rotation, antalgic gait, crepitusOsteoarthritis
Trendelenburg positiveGluteus medius/minimus weakness (superior gluteal nerve, OA, DDH)
Lateral hip tenderness over the greater trochanterGreater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteal tendinopathy, bursitis)
Shortened, externally rotated leg after a fallNeck of femur fracture
Limping child: 4–8 yearsPerthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head)
Limping overweight adolescent (10–15), knee pain, reduced internal rotationSlipped upper femoral epiphysis
Burning anterolateral thigh numbnessMeralgia paraesthetica (lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh)
KneeImmediate swelling after a twisting injury, "pop"Haemarthrosis: ACL tear (positive Lachman's)
Delayed swelling, medial joint line tenderness, positive McMurray's, lockingMeniscal tear (bucket-handle if locked)
Valgus laxity at 20–30°MCL injury
Posterior sagPCL injury
Varus deformity, crepitus, reduced flexion, bony swellingMedial compartment OA
Anterior knee pain on stairs/squatting in a young personPatellofemoral pain
Tender tibial tuberosity in an adolescentOsgood–Schlatter disease
Popliteal swellingBaker's cyst (rupture mimics DVT)
Hot, swollen kneeSeptic arthritis, gout, pseudogout (CPPD: older, chondrocalcinosis)
Wrist/hand, foot/ankleSee weeks 228 and 237

los.text: Formulate an appropriate plan for further investigation or referral, based on clinical findings and current guidelines.
los.html:
SituationInvestigation / referral
Osteoarthritis (≥45, activity-related pain, stiffness ≤30 min)
  • Clinical diagnosis (no imaging needed, NICE NG226)
  • Exercise, weight loss, education
  • Topical NSAIDs (knee, hand), oral NSAID + PPI shortest time
  • Intra-articular steroid short-term
  • Refer for joint replacement when symptoms substantially affect quality of life despite non-surgical care
Acute knee injury
  • X-ray if Ottawa knee rules (age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, can't flex to 90°, can't weight-bear 4 steps)
  • MRI for ligaments/menisci
  • Locked knee → urgent orthopaedics
  • ACL → physio ± reconstruction
Hot swollen jointAspirate before antibiotics (Gram stain, culture, crystals); septic arthritis → emergency
Suspected hip fractureX-ray (AP pelvis + lateral hip), MRI if occult; surgery within 36 h
Child with a limp
  • Urgent assessment
  • Kocher criteria for septic arthritis (non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5 °C, ESR >40, WCC >12)
  • X-ray (frog-leg lateral for SUFE), ultrasound for effusion
Inflammatory arthritisUrgent rheumatology
Red flags (night pain, mass, weight loss)Urgent X-ray; suspected sarcoma/cancer pathway
Scaphoid injuryImmobilise, fracture clinic, MRI if X-ray normal
PhysiotherapyMost soft tissue and degenerative problems, post-injury rehabilitation

los.text: Clearly and concisely present clinical findings from a musculoskeletal examination using appropriate medical terminology and structure.
los.html:
Concise structureJoint and side → key positives → relevant negatives → neurovascular status → summary → plan.
Example (knee)
  • "I examined Mr Y's left knee.
  • He walks with an antalgic gait.
  • There is a moderate effusion on the patellar tap and medial joint line tenderness.
  • Flexion is limited to 100° with a block to full extension.
  • McMurray's test reproduces medial pain with a click; Lachman's and drawer tests are normal and the collaterals are stable.
  • He is neurovascularly intact.
  • In summary, these findings suggest a medial meniscal tear, possibly bucket-handle given the extension block.
  • I'd arrange an urgent MRI and orthopaedic referral."

los.text: Predict the effects of pathology on the anatomy of the gastrointestinal tract
los.html:
PathologyAnatomical basisEffects you can predict
Oesophageal cancerLower third (adenocarcinoma, Barrett's) or middle (squamous); three narrowings
  • Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids)
  • Spread to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarse), trachea (fistula)
  • Lymph to mediastinal and coeliac nodes
Hiatus herniaStomach through the oesophageal hiatus (T10); crura weakReflux (lost sphincter angle), rolling type can strangulate
Peptic ulcerPosterior duodenal ulcer next to the gastroduodenal artery; anterior ulcer faces the peritoneal cavityPosterior: massive bleeding; anterior: perforation → air under the diaphragm, peritonitis, shoulder-tip pain
Gastric cancerLymph via the thoracic ductVirchow's node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilicus), Krukenberg (ovaries)
Pancreatic head cancerCBD passes through the headPainless obstructive jaundice, palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier), duodenal obstruction
GallstonesHartmann's pouch, cystic duct, CBD, ampullaColic, cholecystitis (Murphy's sign), obstructive jaundice, gallstone pancreatitis, gallstone ileus (fistula to duodenum, stuck at the ileocaecal valve)
AppendicitisMidgut visceral pain (T10) then parietal peritoneum (somatic)Periumbilical pain shifting to the RIF; retrocaecal → psoas sign; pelvic → urinary and rectal symptoms
Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernias)Narrow points: hernial necks (femoral below and lateral to the pubic tubercle)Colicky pain, vomiting, distension; dilated loops with valvulae conniventes across the whole width
Large bowel obstruction (cancer, volvulus)Sigmoid on a long mesentery; competent ileocaecal valveClosed loop: caecum dilates most and may perforate (>9–12 cm); haustra don't cross the full width; "coffee-bean" sigmoid volvulus
Colorectal cancerWatershed and lymph follow arteriesRight: anaemia, mass; left: change in bowel habit, obstruction; rectal: bleeding, tenesmus; liver metastases via the portal vein
Diverticular diseaseMucosa herniates where vessels pierce the sigmoid wall (no complete longitudinal muscle: taeniae)LIF pain, bleeding, abscess, fistula (bladder: pneumaturia)
Ischaemic colitisWatershed areas: splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and rectosigmoid (Sudeck's point)Pain and bloody diarrhoea in older vascular patients
Portal hypertensionPortosystemic anastomosesOesophageal varices, caput medusae, rectal varices, splenomegaly, ascites
HaemorrhoidsAnal cushions above the pectinate line (visceral nerves)Painless bright red bleeding; perianal haematoma below the line is painful
Anal fissure / perianal abscessBelow the pectinate line (somatic, pudendal); ischioanal fossaVery painful; abscesses track to the ischioanal fossa, horseshoe round the back
